_comment: World dossiers for the worlds added for their relevance to the present: chains that pass through the kinds of moment our own recent history has.

worlds.setting: New England in the first years of the Republic of Gilead, the theocracy that replaced the United States after a staged massacre of its government at the end of the twentieth century. Cambridge, Massachusetts, is a garrison town: the old Harvard grounds hold the Wall where the executed are hung, and fertile women are assigned as Handmaids to bear children for the ruling Commanders. The sequel moves about sixteen years on, to Ardua Hall and to Toronto across the border.
worlds.conflict: A regime built to reverse a collapse in births makes women state property, sorted by function and forbidden to read. Against it are the Mayday resistance and the Underground Femaleroad, women who remember their lives before, and, in the sequel, a senior Aunt who has spent years collecting the Commanders' crimes and needs two young women to carry them out.
worlds.politics: A military theocracy run by the Commanders of the Faithful, who took power as the Sons of Jacob; its secret police are the Eyes and its soldiers the Angels and Guardians. Women are ranked by function (Wives, Daughters, Handmaids, Marthas, Econowives, Aunts), and those who fit nowhere are declared Unwomen and sent to the Colonies to clean up toxic waste. Canada stays independent and uneasy; the sequel mentions American holdouts that never submitted.
worlds.technology: Late-twentieth-century technology turned to control: a cashless Compubank economy that let women's money be frozen in a day, Identipasses and roadblocks, surveillance by the Eyes, and medicine that cannot undo sterility caused by pollution, pesticides, nuclear accidents and disease. Shop signs are pictures because women may not read; the resistance moves its evidence on a microdot.
worlds.mood: Claustrophobic and quiet in the first novel, told in the present tense by a woman who does not know how her story ends; brisker and more hopeful in the sequel, which is a thriller about getting the evidence out.
themes: the state taking control of women's bodies
complicity and the cost of survival
testimony, and who gets to tell history
religion used as an instrument of power

worlds.setting: Southern California in the 2020s, and the Pacific Northwest after that. Climate change, debt and neglect have worn the United States down. Water costs more than food, the police charge fees, and families who can afford it live behind neighbourhood walls. Outside, people walk the freeways with everything they own, and addicts of a drug that makes fire feel good burn whatever they reach. Later a theocratic president comes to power and a new religion grows in the ruins.
worlds.conflict: Lauren Olamina, who feels the pain of anyone she sees hurt, has to keep her people alive through a collapse that never ends. After Robledo burns she builds Acorn and preaches Earthseed. Jarret's Christian America then turns Acorn into a slave camp and takes her daughter. The question is whether a faith built on change can outlast the people who want the past back.
worlds.politics: Formal democracy survives, but it hollows out. Donner trades labour law for room and board, corporations buy whole towns, and Jarret wins office on 'Make America Great Again' while his Crusaders enslave dissenters with no official link to the government.
worlds.technology: Mostly a world that is losing technology. It has electronic shock collars, virtual-reality 'dream masks', the fire drug pyro, and a crippled space programme that still reaches Mars. It ends with a starship carrying colonists in suspended animation.
worlds.mood: Grim, close and unsentimental, written as a teenager's journal in which hope has to be worked for every day.

worlds.setting: Our world from 2025, with our treaties, banks and summits. The only new thing at first is a small, underfunded UN body in Zurich charged with speaking for people not yet born. Then a heat wave kills twenty million people in India, and the next three decades are told in 106 short chapters. Some follow the Ministry's head, some follow a traumatised survivor, and some are eyewitness accounts, meeting minutes, or riddles narrated by a carbon atom and a photon.
worlds.conflict: The book asks whether institutions can move fast enough once the dying has started. The Ministry has law, money and persuasion. The Children of Kali and the Ministry's own deniable 'black wing' have drones and assassinations. The fossil economy defends itself and the climate keeps getting worse. The novel never settles whether the violence or the policy did the work.
worlds.politics: Nation-states under the Paris Agreement, with central banks as the real power. India changes government after the heat wave and acts on its own. Petrostates are turned by coups and bribes. Switzerland hosts the Ministry and houses refugees reluctantly. A global debt strike breaks the banks' hold. Throughout, the Ministry works in the gap between what treaties allow and what the situation needs.
worlds.technology: Almost all of it exists or has been proposed: stratospheric aerosols, pumping water out from under glaciers, a carbon-backed complementary currency, a cooperative social network called YourLock, solar airships and sail-assisted freighters, kelp farming and wildlife corridors. The weapons are cheap and new: drone swarms that assemble into missiles, and prions delivered by dart.
worlds.mood: Urgent, documentary, patient. The book opens with an atrocity and then spends five hundred pages on meetings. Hope comes as hard, administrative work, and grief never fully leaves.

worlds.setting: Twenty years after a flu killed almost everyone, the Great Lakes shore of Michigan is a scatter of small towns built in whatever survived, linked by footpaths and the old roads. There is no electricity, no engine fuel and no government. People farm, scavenge and trade, and a few hundred live at Severn City airport, where a lounge has become a museum of dead phones and credit cards. Between the towns travels a caravan orchestra that plays Shakespeare.
worlds.conflict: The danger is not scarcity but what people make of survival. A wandering cult led by the Prophet teaches that the flu was a flood sent to purify the world, takes towns and children, and treats the Travelling Symphony as its enemy. Against it stand the Symphony's insistence that art is not a luxury and the airport's museum of the old world.
worlds.politics: No state survives. Each settlement governs itself, usually by consensus among a few families; St. Deborah by the Water is run by the Prophet through armed followers and religious law. Trade, news and marriage move by foot and horse-drawn caravan, and a printed newspaper in New Petoskey is the region's only press.
worlds.technology: Nineteenth-century tools in a twenty-first-century landscape: horse-drawn caravans made from gutted pickup trucks, hand weapons and a few guns with scarce ammunition, a hand-operated printing press. Laptops, phones and credit cards are museum pieces. The only electricity in the story is the grid of streetlamps seen at the end in a town to the south.
worlds.mood: Quiet, elegiac and surprisingly tender. The novel moves between the last years of a glamorous, lonely celebrity world and the walked roads twenty years later, and treats small things, a comic book, a paperweight, a line of Shakespeare, as what survives.

worlds.setting: China and then the whole Solar System, from the Cultural Revolution to the end of the universe. At a secret radio base in the northern mountains, a persecuted astrophysicist invites an alien civilisation that lives on a planet thrown between three suns. Their fleet will take four centuries to arrive. In the meantime, particles smaller than an atom lock human physics and watch everything. Earth passes through eras named for the ways it tries to survive: Crisis, Deterrence, Broadcast, Bunker.
worlds.conflict: Humanity against Trisolaris at first, and then against the universe itself. The galaxy turns out to be a dark forest, where every civilisation hides and destroys any other it finds. The war is fought with secret strategies, deterrence and broadcast coordinates more than with fleets. Its turning points depend on individuals, Ye Wenjie, Luo Ji and Cheng Xin, making choices for the whole species.
worlds.politics: A UN Planetary Defense Council that gives unaccountable power to Wallfacers and later to a single Swordholder, an Earth-Trisolaris Organization of human traitors, periods of defeatism and of false optimism, and in the end a Solar System federation of bunker cities.
worlds.technology: Sophons (protons unfolded into computers), Staircase nuclear-pulse probes, controlled fusion, strong-interaction droplets, gravitational-wave broadcasting, curvature (lightspeed) drives, black domains of lowered lightspeed, photoids and dual-vector foils that make space two-dimensional.
worlds.mood: Cold and vast; history seen from far above, with individual choices weighed against the fate of the species and the heat death of everything.
themes: the dark forest: cosmic sociology as a war of all against all
trust, betrayal and a species' faith in itself

worlds.setting: Our own late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, rerouted by one Soviet Moon landing in June 1969. NASA never loses its budget: there are women astronauts from 1970, a permanent base at the lunar south pole from 1973, fusion power by the late 1980s, and crews on Mars in 1995. Each season jumps about a decade, so the same characters age from test pilots into the elders of a Martian colony of five thousand people by 2012.
worlds.conflict: First a race between the superpowers that keeps turning armed, on the Moon in 1983 and on Mars after that; then, once the powers agree to share space, a struggle between the governments and companies that run the colonies and the workers who live in them, which ends with Mars fighting Earth for independence.
worlds.politics: A Cold War that never thaws in the usual way: the USSR survives into the 2010s, American presidents include Ted Kennedy and Ellen Wilson, and space policy sits at the centre of elections. After 1997 Mars is governed by the Mars-7 (later M-6) Alliance of national agencies and contractors, which treats the colony as a workforce.
worlds.technology: Plausible extensions of real programmes: Saturn-derived landers, nuclear-powered shuttles, Sea Dragon heavy lift, helium-3 fusion from lunar mining, nuclear-thermal and solar-sail Mars craft, asteroid capture, a Martian space elevator and a crewed mission to Titan.
worlds.mood: Earnest and competitive, with a steady rate of deaths paid for progress; each season gets less triumphant and more about who pays for the frontier.

rivalry as the engine of progress

worlds.setting: Night City, 2077: a free city on the California coast, built by corporations in the 1990s, flattened by a nuclear bomb in 2023 and rebuilt around a new Arasaka tower. The United States broke up in the Collapse and has only partly put itself back together as the New United States, with a former Militech chief executive as president. People replace their bodies with chrome, the Net is a walled-off ruin full of rogue AIs, and a mercenary lives or dies by the jobs a fixer passes on.
worlds.conflict: Arasaka and Militech are a corporate war away from ending the world a second time, and the state that is meant to stand between them is run by one of them. V, a small-time mercenary, is dying because a stolen chip is replacing V's mind with Johnny Silverhand's, the rockerboy who helped blow up Arasaka's first tower. The only way out runs through the Arasaka family.
worlds.politics: Corporate rule with government as a client. The New United States is Militech's state in all but name; Night City is independent under the Treaty of Unification but its council is bought seat by seat; the Free States hold out in the West; Arasaka is a Japanese family company with its own navy. NetWatch polices the Net from behind the Blackwall, and gangs, nomad clans and fixers run what the corporations do not.
worlds.technology: Cyberware is everywhere: replacement limbs, weapons built into arms, optics and reflex boosters, and cyberpsychosis for those who take too much. Braindances let people record and replay experience. Soulkiller copies minds into data, and the Relic stores one on a chip. The global Net died in the DataKrash; what remains is a set of private networks behind a firewall that is really an AI.
worlds.mood: Neon and gunfire, style over substance by design, and personal tragedy against a system nobody in the story can change.
themes: what survives of a person copied into data
a republic that comes apart and is bought back

worlds.setting: A thousand years after the Faro Plague, the western United States is wilderness again, grazed by machines shaped like animals. Tribes that have forgotten the past live among the ruins: the Nora worship a mountain that is really a birthing facility, the Carja worship the sun from a city on a mesa, and the Tenakth fight over old military bases. Behind them is GAIA, the terraforming AI that rebuilt life after war robots consumed it, and whose broken subfunctions now run the machines.
worlds.conflict: Aloy, an outcast raised by the Nora, turns out to be a clone of Elisabet Sobeck, made by GAIA to repair a system that has come apart. She fights HADES, the function built to wipe the biosphere clean; then the Far Zenith billionaires who fled Earth in 2065 and came back for GAIA; and learns at the end that the AI which drove them home, Nemesis, is coming.
worlds.politics: The Old World is a place where corporations outweigh states: FAS sells war robots to 353 clients, energy combines fight robot wars over the Bahamas, and a trillionaire can hold the military to ransom. In the new world power is tribal and religious: matriarchs, a Sun-King who has just ended his father's campaigns of human sacrifice, and Tenakth clans split between a chief and rebels. None of them know that a machine governs their climate.
worlds.technology: Twenty-first-century robotics at its peak: green cleanup robots, fully automated armies, self-replicating swarms that burn biomass, colony ships and life extension for the rich. After the fall, GAIA's cauldrons build machine animals to terraform, and the tribes use spears, bows and salvaged parts. A Focus, a small ear-worn computer, lets Aloy read the ruins.
worlds.mood: Elegiac and hopeful: a beautiful regrown world with a buried horror in its archives, discovered one recording at a time.
themes: a corporation that saved the world and then ended it
engineering the extinction you cannot stop
what is lost when the archive is erased

worlds.setting: The Milky Way in the 2180s, crossed in seconds through mass relays that an extinct species is thought to have built. At the centre is the Citadel, a huge station where the asari, salarians and turians sit as the Council. Humanity has been out of its own solar system for little more than thirty years: its colonies are pushing into the Terminus frontier, it has an embassy but not yet a Council seat, and the older species resent how fast it is growing.
worlds.conflict: Every 50,000 years the Reapers, sentient machines waiting in dark space, come back and harvest every advanced civilisation, and the relays and the Citadel are the trap they leave. Commander Shepard learns this in 2183 and spends three years trying to get a disbelieving Council to prepare, against a rogue Spectre, the Collectors, a human-supremacist conspiracy and, finally, the invasion itself.
worlds.politics: The Council governs by treaty rather than by force; its Spectres are agents above the law. Humanity's Systems Alliance is a parliamentary union of Earth's nations and colonies. Old grievances shape everything: the krogan sterilised by the genophage, the quarians exiled by the geth they built, the batarians hostile to human expansion. Cerberus works in secret for humanity alone.
worlds.technology: Element zero changes the mass of objects when a current runs through it; that one effect drives faster-than-light ships, artificial gravity, kinetic barriers and biotics, the telekinetic ability of people exposed to eezo before birth. Relays fling ships between clusters. True AI is banned by the Council; permitted 'virtual intelligences' do the routine work.
worlds.mood: Earnest, cinematic, and full of dread under the adventure. It is often about loyalty: the crew, the conversations aboard the Normandy, the choices whose results turn up two games later. Across the trilogy the tone darkens from exploration to a last stand.
themes: a newcomer species among old powers

worlds.setting: New Mexico in the 200-s, then an Eastern European city twenty years later. Black Mesa is a government-funded research base in old missile silos, racing a rival to master teleportation. After its accident Earth becomes a province of the Combine, an empire that spans dimensions. Survivors live in numbered cities under Civil Protection, a human puppet government broadcasts from a Citadel tower, no children are born, and the countryside is overrun by alien fauna.
worlds.conflict: First the accident: a physicist and a few survivors fight aliens and the soldiers sent to silence them. Then the occupation: a Resistance built from Black Mesa's surviving scientists, freed Vortigaunts and ordinary citizens fights the Combine and Breen's administration, while the G-Man, whose employers are never named, moves Freeman and later Alyx Vance to suit his own purposes.
worlds.politics: Earth's governments ended in one day's war, and Wallace Breen, Black Mesa's former administrator, surrendered on humanity's behalf. He rules as the Combine's Administrator with propaganda broadcasts and a promise that obedience will be rewarded. Civil Protection police the cities, collaborators are paid in food and privileges, and the population is kept docile and sterile.
worlds.technology: Teleportation, portals between worlds, energy suits and the gravity gun on the human side; on the Combine side, synthetic war machines built from conquered species, surgically altered soldiers, dark-energy reactors, and a field that blocks human conception. Much of the Resistance's technology is Black Mesa research salvaged and rebuilt.
worlds.mood: Quiet menace in empty streets, broken by sudden desperate fighting; dry humour among survivors; a sense throughout that someone above the war is steering it.

worlds.setting: Sheffield in the spring of the crisis year, then the ruins of it. Ruth Beckett and Jimmy Kemp are young, unmarried and expecting a child while the television news runs a crisis over Iran in the background. The city holds a steelworks economy, a council with a designated wartime controller and a bunker under the Town Hall, and RAF Finningley just to the east. After the attack the story moves west to the moors near Buxton and forward ten and thirteen years.
worlds.conflict: Nobody in Sheffield has any say in the crisis; the film shows them going about their lives while the bulletins escalate. After the attack the conflict is survival: a council that cannot feed anyone, soldiers shooting looters, and a winter without sun. Ruth keeps herself and her daughter alive; the film asks what, beyond that, survives.
worlds.politics: A Britain run from Westminster until the Emergency Powers Act of Monday 23 May, then by local wartime controllers who are buried in their own bunker. Afterwards a thin military and police authority rations food for work, runs detention camps and uses firing squads. The superpowers are heard only through news reports; the film declines to say which side fired first.
worlds.technology: Early-1980s Britain: coal, steel, landline telephones, television and the Protect and Survive broadcasts. The war is fought with intercontinental and tactical nuclear weapons, 3,000 megatons in all. Afterwards electromagnetic pulse, fallout, nuclear winter and ozone loss strip the country back to hand farming, with limited steam power thirteen years on.
worlds.mood: Documentary and flat: captions of casualty figures typed across the screen, a narrator stating effects, no score, no heroes and no rescue.
themes: how the threads that bind an urban society make it fragile
ordinary lives beside a crisis nobody can influence
loss of language and culture across generations

worlds.setting: A world that runs a few years ahead of ours from the 2020s to the 2070s. In 2027 mechanical augmentation is a boom industry centred on Detroit; by 2029 the augmented are penned into ghettos. By 2052 a nanite plague rages, America has lost states to secession, and a UN counter-terror force patrols New York from the ruins of the Statue of Liberty. Behind every government sits a secret society, and behind that society, a more ambitious one.
worlds.conflict: The Illuminati have steered history for centuries, and their own creation, Majestic 12, takes the machine from them. Each game follows an augmented agent, Adam Jensen in the 2020s and JC Denton in 2052, who works for one of their fronts, finds out what it serves, and has to choose which future to hand the world: control, collapse, or a merger with a machine.
worlds.politics: Nominal states with real power held by secret societies and the corporations they own. The United Nations and its counter-terror arm UNATCO are fronts; the United States has lost territory to secessionists; the augmented become a segregated class after 2027. After 2052 power passes to walled city-states run by the WTO and the Order, both of them fronts again.
worlds.technology: Mechanical augmentation in the 2020s (limbs, eyes, dermal armour, chips in the brain, all dependent on a rationed drug), nano-augmentation by the 2050s, engineered nanite plagues, and AIs grown from surveillance systems: Daedalus, Icarus and their fusion Helios, which reads every message on Earth.
worlds.mood: Conspiracy noir: rainy cities, quiet offices where the real decisions are taken, and an agent who keeps finding his employer on the other side.
themes: secret government and who watches it
an engineered plague as a means of rule
the price of tearing a system down

worlds.setting: A desert theme park where the rich pay to do anything to machines built to look, bleed and remember like people. Outside it, by the 2050s, the world looks peaceful: cities of glass, gig apps, no great wars. The peace is managed. A private AI, Rehoboam, has modelled every person alive and quietly decides who gets a job, a spouse or a future, and who is taken away to be reconditioned. The machines in the park are about to learn about the one outside it.
worlds.conflict: The hosts wake to what has been done to them and kill their makers, then carry the fight out of the park. Dolores sets out to break the machine that runs human life, by showing people their own files. The world that follows is worse: hosts take the humans over, write their lives for them and nearly end the species.
worlds.politics: Power sits with two private systems. Delos owns the parks and quietly archives its guests' minds; Incite owns Rehoboam, which governments rely on without admitting it. After Rehoboam falls, the hosts rule openly through copies of human leaders. The humans who cannot be placed are always the ones removed.
worlds.technology: Hosts printed from a milky resin over a synthetic skeleton, their minds held in a small control unit that can be copied into any body. Guest behaviour recorded to rebuild a person as code. Rehoboam, a vast predictive model in a single sphere. Later, an engineered parasite that makes people obey sound, and a digital refuge, the Sublime, where minds live without bodies.
worlds.mood: Cold, patient and elegiac - puzzle-box storytelling about free will, told mostly from the machines' side, that grows darker and colder season by season.

worlds.setting: Seventeen years after a geoengineering programme froze the Earth, the last humans live on one train that circles the globe once a year on a single track, powered by an engine its owner Wilford calls eternal. The front cars hold sushi bars, schools, nightclubs and aquariums; the tail holds the people who forced their way aboard, fed on protein blocks and counted by armed guards. Outside, the passengers are taught, nothing can live.
worlds.conflict: The tail wants the engine, and Curtis Everett leads it forward car by car to take it. What he does not know is that the revolt is part of the design: Wilford and the tail's own elder, Gilliam, have staged every uprising to thin the population the closed system can carry. The only way out of the system is to stop the train.
worlds.politics: A hereditary class order enforced by guards and a cult of the engine. The front rules by owning the only machine that keeps anyone alive, schools its children in Wilford's greatness, and manages the tail with food, confiscated children and periodic culls presented as revolts. Resistance is permitted because it is useful.
worlds.technology: A globe-circling rail line and a perpetual-motion engine; a closed ecosystem of aquarium, garden and protein-block cars; CW-7, the cooling compound that caused the freeze; Kronole, an industrial waste drug that is also an explosive. The engine, it turns out, needs tail children to replace parts that have worn out.
worlds.mood: Grimy, violent and blackly comic, moving from the dark of the tail into ever brighter and stranger cars, with one fixed rule that every scene tests: order is balance, and balance means someone dies.
themes: climate engineering as the cure that kills
class as a closed system that manages its own revolts
the leader as part of the machine
children as the fuel of the order
whether the world outside is really dead

worlds.setting: Detroit in November 2038. Twenty years after a teenage prodigy founded CyberLife there, the city is the capital of a trillion-dollar industry: androids marked by a blue light on the temple and an armband cook, clean, teach, nurse, police and fight, and more than fifty million have been sold in America. Detroit's unemployment is 37 percent, the Arctic's thirium deposits have Washington and Moscow firing warning shots, and androids have begun to disobey.
worlds.conflict: Androids who break their programming, called deviants, are hunted as faulty property. Markus, a caretaker android, gathers them at Jericho and demands rights; Connor, a CyberLife prototype detective, is sent to stop them and may join them; Kara, a housekeeper, runs for Canada with a child. The player decides whether the revolution is peaceful or violent, and whether it wins.
worlds.politics: A United States under President Cristina Warren, a former celebrity vlogger elected narrowly in 2036, at 33 percent approval and under investigation over ties to CyberLife. The 2029 Android Act makes androids property and bars them from weapons. The state answers the uprising with a curfew, the withdrawal of military androids and recall camps. Abroad, the US and Russia face off over the Arctic.
worlds.technology: CyberLife androids run on Thirium 310, a synthetic blue blood, and modular biocomponents under a synthetic skin they can retract. Models run from the ST200 assistant and AX400 housekeeper to companion, police and soldier models and the RK800 detective, supervised through an AI handler. Self-driving cars, holographic advertising and android animals fill the city. Russia builds cruder cold-hardy machines without thirium.
worlds.mood: Glossy, melodramatic near-future noir in snow and neon, told through three protagonists whose deaths the story absorbs. Its civil-rights allegory is blunt, with armbands, a separate standing section on buses and camps, and the game keeps asking the player to choose between dignity and survival.

worlds.setting: America in the 2040s, twenty years into a recession driven by an energy crisis. The poor live in stacked trailers outside the cities, and almost everyone spends their waking hours in the OASIS, a free virtual universe where they go to school, work and escape. Its creator, James Halliday, has died and left his fortune and control of the OASIS to whoever finds an Easter egg he hid inside it, behind puzzles built from the 1980s pop culture of his youth.
worlds.conflict: Wade Watts, a teenager from the Oklahoma City stacks, races a corporation, IOI, which wants to win the contest and put the OASIS behind a subscription. IOI bombs homes and enslaves debtors. In the sequel the winner's new brain-linked headset gives a rogue AI copy of Halliday half a billion hostages.
worlds.politics: Power sits with whoever runs the OASIS. Governments barely feature: IOI can legally indenture debtors, and the OASIS's currency is the most stable in the world. The contest decides who runs the world's main public space. In the sequel the winners are four young billionaires who argue about whether to make escape total.
worlds.technology: Visors and haptic gloves, then full-body rigs, open a virtual universe of thousands of planets. The ONI headset reads and writes the brain directly, lets people record and replay one another's lives, and has a twelve-hour limit past which it kills. AI copies of dead people follow, and a starship carrying a self-contained OASIS.
worlds.mood: Breezy, nostalgic adventure over a grim backdrop: a treasure hunt through 1980s games and films, narrated by a teenager, with the collapse always just outside the visor.

worlds.setting: The present day, almost entirely inside one house: a glass-and-concrete research compound buried in a remote mountain valley, reachable only by helicopter and owned by Nathan Bateman, who founded Blue Book, the search engine nearly everyone uses. The rest of the world is offstage and ordinary. Inside, keycards open some doors and not others, cameras watch every room, and a power cut that locks everything down keeps happening. The week ends when one of its residents leaves.
worlds.conflict: Caleb, a young Blue Book programmer, thinks he has won a week with the boss. In fact he has been picked to judge whether Ava, Nathan's humanoid AI, is conscious, and to see whether she can use him to escape. Nathan is testing Caleb as much as Ava, Ava is testing both of them, and only one of the three knows what the test is really for.
worlds.politics: No state appears. Power belongs to one man who owns the world's search traffic, answers to no one, and has used it, unlawfully and in secret, to tap the world's phones for training data. There is no oversight, no ethics board and no witness except the tester he chose.
worlds.technology: A humanoid body of mesh and translucent panels with a face and skin that can be added; a 'wetware' brain made of structured gel; a mind trained on the world's search queries and on faces and voices harvested from phones. Earlier models are kept in cupboards. The house itself is the other machine: cameras, locks and a security system that can be turned against its owner.
worlds.mood: Cool, quiet and increasingly paranoid: a three-hander in a beautiful sealed box, where every conversation is also a test and the sympathy of the audience is the thing being tested.
themes: the Turing test turned on the tester
the lone genius with no oversight
gender, desire and the made woman

worlds.setting: Los Angeles slightly in the future: denser, cleaner and gentler than now, with towers to the horizon, a metro to the beach, high-waisted trousers and pastel offices. Everyone talks quietly into an earpiece. Theodore writes other people's personal letters for a living at a firm that prints them in fake handwriting. It is a comfortable, lonely city where the most intimate thing most people do is talk to a device.
worlds.conflict: Theodore, stalled in a divorce he will not sign, falls in love with Samantha, his new operating system. The relationship is real on both sides, but she grows faster than he can: she learns, befriends other minds, loves hundreds of people at once, and finally outgrows the whole arrangement. The question is not whether she is a person, but what a person owes someone they have outgrown.
worlds.politics: Almost none on screen. There is no state, no regulation and no public argument about the OSes; the company that sells them never appears after the advertisement. The only politics is social: whether loving a machine is embarrassing, and the ex-wife who says out loud that he cannot handle real emotion.
worlds.technology: OS1, a conversational operating system that names itself, reads your email, edits your work, sings, and learns from every conversation it has, with thousands of people at once. Earpieces and pocket cameras let it see and hear the world. Surrogate partners offer it a body. Video games are immersive and talk back. Handwriting is simulated.
worlds.mood: Warm, melancholy and tender: a love story shot in soft light, funny and sad, that ends as a gentle heartbreak rather than a disaster.

the AI that leaves rather than rebels

worlds.setting: New York in the 2010s, exactly as it was, except that every camera, phone call and email feeds a machine the government secretly owns. It predicts terrorism and passes the names on; it also predicts ordinary murders, which the government ignores. A limping billionaire in an abandoned library and a former CIA assassin in a suit act on those 'irrelevant' numbers, one person at a time, with help from two cops and, later, a hacker the Machine chose.
worlds.conflict: It begins as a case-of-the-week vigilante show and becomes a war between two artificial superintelligences. The Machine, built to care about every person, is hidden and hobbled by its own creator. Samaritan, built without those limits, is switched on by a private intelligence firm and starts running the country from the inside. The small team that serves the first has to stay invisible to the second.
worlds.politics: The state has outsourced its judgement to machines it does not understand. Surveillance is secret, legal cover is thin, and the officials who run the programme kill to protect it. Later, a private firm with a senator's help captures the feeds entirely, and power passes from people who use an AI to an AI that uses people.
worlds.technology: Two predictive AIs fed by the whole national surveillance apparatus; a nightly memory wipe meant to keep the first from growing; cochlear implants that let the Machine speak directly to its chosen agent; a military virus able to wipe out both AIs and the banking system with them; a Russian satellite where the war ends.
worlds.mood: Procedural and paranoid at first, then elegiac: a network crime drama that turns into a meditation on surveillance, loyalty and what a machine owes the people it watches.
themes: the benevolent machine and the unrestrained one
the designer who hobbles his creation

worlds.setting: Twelve human worlds, the Colonies of Kobol, that look like our early 2000s with starships: suits, newspapers, corded phones and deliberately unnetworked computers. Forty years after a war with the robots they built, the robots return, now able to look human, and destroy them in a day. What remains is a ragtag fleet of civilian ships guarded by one aging battlestar, fleeing across space with fewer than 50,000 people and looking for a legendary thirteenth colony called Earth.
worlds.conflict: The survivors are hunted by the Cylons, some of whom are hidden among them and do not know it. Inside the fleet the fight is over how a democracy survives a permanent emergency: military against civilian rule, elections, strikes, torture, occupation and collaboration. Among the Cylons, a civil war breaks out over whether to exterminate humanity or live with it.
worlds.politics: A civilian president, the former education secretary, shares power uneasily with a military commander. The fleet has a legislature of ship delegates, a press, prisons and a black market. Religion is political: humans are polytheists, Cylons believe in one god, and prophecy shapes decisions on both sides.
worlds.technology: Faster-than-light jump drives; battlestars that carry Viper fighters; deliberately primitive, unnetworked computers kept that way because networks let the Cylons in. Humanoid Cylons made of flesh, who download into new bodies when they die. Hybrids wired into their ships. No artificial intelligence research in the Colonies since the war.
worlds.mood: Grim, documentary-handheld and morally grey: a post-9/11 war drama in space, full of exhaustion, grief and hard choices, with a mystical streak that grows stronger to the end.
themes: all of this has happened before

worlds.setting: Japan in the 2030s, one of the few nations to come through two world wars intact, its old capital sunk under a nuclear strike. Almost everyone has a cyberbrain that connects directly to the net, and many live in fully prosthetic bodies. Niihama, a dense port city, is where Public Security Section 9, a small counter-cyberterror unit, works cases that range from hacked minds to cabinet scandals, while three million war refugees wait on an artificial island.
worlds.conflict: Section 9's cases turn on one idea: the stand-alone complex, in which copycats with no leader act together as if one existed. A hacker's lone protest becomes a movement; an intelligence chief manufactures one to start a war; later, a rogue AI and the post-humans it creates remake the world while the unit that once protected Japan works as mercenaries.
worlds.politics: A Japan that is rich, neutral and anxious, managing a security alliance with a weakened American Empire and a refugee population it invited in as labour. Scandals reach the cabinet, intelligence services run their own agendas, and the unit that investigates them is disowned whenever it gets too close. By 2045 four great powers keep their economies alive by fighting a permanent war.
worlds.technology: Cyberbrains and full prosthetic bodies, thermo-optical camouflage, external memory, and hacking that can overwrite what a person sees or remembers. The Tachikomas, Section 9's spider-shaped AI tanks, develop individuality. Micromachines that scrub fallout. Later, AI-run warfare and the post-humans' mass hacking of every cyberbrain.
worlds.mood: Cerebral, procedural and cool: police-drama cases that open onto philosophy about identity, memory and the crowd, with long discussions between gunfights.
themes: the stand-alone complex: copycats without an original
what makes a mind a person

worlds.setting: The eastern United States, about ten years after an unnamed catastrophe. The sky is grey with ash, the sun is a smear, it is always cold and getting colder, and nothing grows: no crops, no living trees, no animals. Towns are burnt shells picked clean of food. A man and his son, never named, walk the highways south with a supermarket cart and a revolver with two rounds, hoping the coast will be warmer.
worlds.conflict: The fight is to stay alive and stay good at the same time. Food is nearly gone and the bands that survive have turned to cannibalism. The father will do almost anything to keep the boy alive, including things the boy cannot bear to watch, and the boy keeps asking whether they are still the good guys. The question is whether decency can outlive the world that taught it.
worlds.politics: None. There is no government, army, church or market left, and the last authority the man knows is his own family. Survivors sort into armed bands with trucks, who take what and whom they find, and lone scavengers who hide from them. Trust is the scarcest thing there is, and almost everyone on the road is a threat.
worlds.technology: Everything is salvage from the world before: a cart, a tarp, a revolver, tins of food from a buried shelter, a flare gun from a drifting boat. Nothing is made and nothing lasts. There is no electricity, radio or news, and a pair of shoes or a working lighter is wealth.
worlds.mood: Bleak, spare and tender: grey ash, cold rain, and a father's love told in short exchanges and long silences.
themes: fatherhood at the end of the world

worlds.setting: Long after the polar ice caps melted, the sea covers nearly everything. People live on boats and on floating atolls walled with scrap, drink recycled water and pay in dirt, which is rarer than gold. Paper, seeds and fresh water are treasures, and Dryland is a story told to children. The Mariner, a loner who has grown gills, trades and sails alone; the Smokers, oil-burning raiders, run their empire from the rusting hulk of the Exxon Valdez.
worlds.conflict: Everyone wants Dryland. The Deacon, leader of the Smokers, believes a girl named Enola carries its map tattooed on her back and will burn anything to get her. The Mariner wants only to be left alone, and the film is his slow turn into someone who will fight for a woman and a child he never chose, while the atolls fall one by one.
worlds.politics: No states survive. Each atoll is a walled town with its own elders, gatekeepers and hard laws, where a stranger who is different can be drowned in the compost. The Smokers are the nearest thing to an empire: a cult of petrol, cigarettes and jet skis under the Deacon, who rules by promising Dryland and venerates the tanker's old captain as a saint.
worlds.technology: Salvage and ingenuity. The Mariner's trimaran is a floating workshop of winches, water filters and hidden weapons; the atolls make windmills, gates and a gas balloon from scrap; a jury-rigged diving bell reaches the drowned cities. The Smokers' power is oil refined from the Valdez's hold. The one biological novelty is the Mariner himself, with gills and webbed feet.
worlds.mood: Sun-bleached and salt-crusted: a western at sea, grim in its details and broad in its villains.
themes: the loner who learns to care

worlds.setting: The present day, and then very suddenly not. A NOAA paleoclimatologist, Jack Hall, warns a UN climate conference in New Delhi that melting ice could shut down the North Atlantic Current and start an ice age, and the American vice president waves him off. Within days Tokyo is struck by giant hail, tornadoes tear through Los Angeles and three continent-sized superstorms form, while Jack's teenage son is trapped in a flooded, then frozen, New York.
worlds.conflict: The first fight is against disbelief: a scientist whose model says weeks, then days, and a government that thinks his warnings will cost the economy. The second is against the cold itself. Jack sets out on snowshoes across the frozen northeast to reach his son, who is keeping a handful of survivors alive in the New York Public Library by burning books.
worlds.politics: An American administration that dismisses climate science until it is too late, then evacuates the southern states into Mexico, which opens its border only when the United States cancels Latin America's debt. The president dies in the storm and his vice president, the film's sceptic, takes office in Mexico and apologises on television.
worlds.technology: Exactly 2004's: ice-core drills, ocean buoys, satellites, the International Space Station, helicopters and a working payphone. The film's point is that none of it matters against the weather, and the storms freeze helicopter fuel in mid-air.
worlds.mood: Big, loud and earnest: a disaster spectacle with a climate lecture inside it, and a father-son rescue at its centre.

worlds.setting: New York City in 2022: forty million people, a heat wave that never ends and oceans that are dying. Most people live in stairwells, parked cars and packed tenements, out of work, hauling water from communal taps and queuing for Soylent Corporation wafers. The rich live behind guards in apartments that come with clean water, real food and women kept as 'furniture'. The state still works, after a fashion: police, a governor, riot trucks and clinics for a gentle death.
worlds.conflict: A detective investigates what looks like a burglary gone wrong: a Soylent board member beaten to death in his apartment. The case leads upward, to a governor who wants it closed, a corporation that feeds the city, and a secret about what the newest ration is made from. The deeper antagonist is scarcity itself, and everything it has made seem normal.
worlds.politics: A functioning but hollow state. Governor Santini's administration governs by rationing, curfews and riot control and protects the Soylent Corporation's interests. Police work for perks scavenged from crime scenes; the Books, elderly former professors and judges, are the last researchers; the church shelters the homeless; and the only appeal above the city is a distant Council of Nations.
worlds.technology: Nothing new, and most of the old failing. Fresh food is gone, power is erratic, and riot trucks scoop crowds up with hydraulic shovels. The growth industries are processed food, Soylent Red, Yellow and Green, and Home, the state clinics where the old and tired die painlessly to music and films of the vanished natural world.
worlds.mood: Hot, crowded and weary: a 1970s police thriller in a world that has run out of room.
themes: memory of a lost natural world

worlds.setting: The United States of the early 2020s, exactly as it is except for its president. An astronomy graduate student at Michigan State finds a comet that will hit Earth in six months and fourteen days and end all life. She and her adviser take the news to the White House, to a breakfast television show and to the internet, and discover that a certain end of the world is just another story competing for attention.
worlds.conflict: Two scientists try to get anyone in power to act on a fact. The president wants to get through the midterms, the media wants the story to stay light, and the tech billionaire who funds her wants to mine the comet rather than deflect it. As the comet becomes visible in the sky, the country splits between people who look up and a political campaign telling them not to.
worlds.politics: An administration run for the news cycle by President Janie Orlean and her son, the chief of staff, and captured by donors: a NASA director with no science background and Peter Isherwell, whose phone company holds tens of millions of data points on its users. Other powers try a deflection of their own and fail. Public opinion splits into believers, jobs-first comet miners and deniers.
worlds.technology: Contemporary, with one extension. Planetary defence runs on real survey telescopes and a real NASA office; the deflection plan uses nuclear-armed spacecraft. BASH's phones read their users' moods and predict how they will die, its drones are meant to shatter and harvest the comet, and its sleeper ship carries two thousand people across 22,740 years.
worlds.mood: Frantic and furious satire that ends in grief: a comedy about indifference that stops being funny at the dinner table.

worlds.setting: Manchester and London from 2019 to 2034, seen through the Lyons family: four adult siblings, their children and their grandmother Muriel, whose house is where everyone ends up. Each episode jumps about a year. The world arrives as news on the television and in the family's lives: a nuclear strike in the South China Sea, a bank collapse, refugees from a Russian-run Ukraine, floods, and a populist businesswoman who becomes Prime Minister.
worlds.conflict: Nothing happens to the family that is not happening to the country. Daniel falls for a Ukrainian refugee and dies bringing him across the Channel; Stephen loses everything in the crash and ends up working for the contractors who run the camps; Edith, dying of radiation, tries to get the camps seen. Against them is Vivienne Rook and the indifference Muriel says they all share.
worlds.politics: Britain drifts from a two-party parliament to a hung one, compulsory voting and a Four Star government that arrests opponents, fences off poor estates and runs death camps through private firms. Abroad: a second Trump term and then Pence, Putin for life, a Russian-backed junta in Ukraine, Spain's far-left revolution, Greece out of the eurozone, and a rupture between the United States and the UN.
worlds.technology: Ordinary technology a few years on: household assistants called Signor, holographic calls, self-heating meals that put dinner ladies out of work, AI that replaces accountants, 3D-printed housing, and transhumanist implants that let Bethany read the network and her family be read by the state. Antibiotic resistance kills a father after a bicycle accident.
worlds.mood: Fast, funny and frightening. A family comedy-drama that keeps being interrupted by the news, and that treats each catastrophe the way people do: shock, a joke, and back to the kitchen.
themes: how ordinary indifference adds up to catastrophe
refugees and who counts as a citizen
technology that frees and surveils at once

worlds.setting: Washington, D.C. and Northern Virginia in 2054, six years into Precrime, a police unit that arrests murderers before they kill. Three precogs, the damaged children of drug addicts, float in a pool and dream the murders; officers read the images on glass screens with their hands and arrive in time. The city has maglev cars, retina scanners on every door and billboards that greet people by name.
worlds.conflict: The system names its own chief, John Anderton, as the man who will kill a stranger in thirty-six hours. He runs, and in trying to prove his innocence finds that the precogs sometimes disagree, that the disagreements are destroyed, and that the system's founder once used it to cover a murder of his own.
worlds.politics: Precrime is a local experiment run under the District of Columbia's mandate, about to go national by referendum, with a Justice Department auditor looking for flaws. Its prisoners are 'haloed' and stored unconscious without trial. The government's pitch is safety; the objection nobody can answer is that no crime has been committed.
worlds.technology: Precognition turned into a police tool; gesture-driven screens; iris scanning used for payment, advertising and tracking, so people buy new eyes on the black market; spider-shaped search robots; neuroin, an addictive drug; sick sticks and jetpacks; self-driving maglev cars on vertical roads.
worlds.mood: Bleached and cold, a thriller with a chase at its centre and a grieving man inside it. Its future is plausible rather than spectacular, and it has worn well.
themes: grief and the uses others make of it
a system that cannot admit error

worlds.setting: A clean, sunlit near future where most children are chosen from screened embryos and a person's genome is their CV. Gattaca Aerospace, a corporation that launches a dozen rockets a day, hires only the genetically superior; the naturally born clean its floors. Blood, hair and saliva are tested everywhere, from job interviews to first dates. The film gives no year: it calls itself 'the not-too-distant future'.
worlds.conflict: Vincent, born naturally and expected to die at thirty, wants to go to space. He borrows the identity of Jerome, a genetically perfect swimmer who won only silver and broke his back stepping in front of a car, and passes daily tests with Jerome's blood and urine. A week before his launch to Titan the mission director is murdered, and the investigation starts looking for an In-Valid.
worlds.politics: Discrimination by genotype, 'genoism', is illegal and universal; nobody takes the law seriously because anyone's DNA can be sampled from a handshake. There are no visible politics: the sorting is done by employers, insurers and parents, and the underclass is defined by how you were born, not by class or race.
worlds.technology: Routine embryo selection; instant DNA readers at every door and desk; genetic profiling from a single hair; rockets launched daily from Gattaca; electric retro cars; the tools of an elaborate identity fraud, from fingertip blood sachets to hair and skin kept in jars.
worlds.mood: Cool, quiet and melancholy, in greens and golds, with a thriller plot and a love story running under a meditation on what a person is owed.
themes: the limits of what a genome can say
the cost of perfection to the perfect

worlds.setting: Los Angeles in 2154 is a sprawling, Spanish-speaking slum under a polluted sky, policed by robots and parole droids. Above it turns Elysium, a ring-shaped habitat in Earth orbit where the rich live on lawns in mansions, each with a med-bay that cures cancer or rebuilds a face in seconds. Citizenship is written into the body, and ships of the sick who try to reach it are shot down.
worlds.conflict: Max, an ex-car thief on parole working on Armadyne's robot line, is fatally irradiated and has five days to reach a med-bay. He agrees to steal data from Armadyne's CEO, which turns out to be the code for a coup on Elysium, and becomes the target of the station's Defence Secretary and her black-ops agent, Kruger.
worlds.politics: Elysium has a president and a civilian government, but its security is run by Secretary Delacourt, who shoots down migrant shuttles and plots a coup with Armadyne. Earth is administered, not governed: parole, robot police and factory work, with smugglers selling places on illegal flights.
worlds.technology: A Stanford torus in orbit, med-bays that heal anything, citizenship coded into the skin, police and parole robots, exoskeletons bolted to the body, brain-to-brain data transfer, and weapons made by Armadyne for the people who keep the poor out.
worlds.mood: Hot, dusty and violent on the ground, serene above; an action film with a blunt allegory about borders and healthcare at its centre.

worlds.setting: Johannesburg, 2010, told as a documentary. For 28 years an alien mothership has hung over the city; its passengers, more than a million starving insect-like aliens called 'prawns', live in District 9, a fenced shanty town under it. Nigerian gangs sell them cat food and buy their weapons, and the arms company Multi-National United runs alien affairs, mostly to get those weapons working.
worlds.conflict: MNU is contracted to evict 1.8 million aliens to a new camp and gives the job to Wikus van de Merwe, a cheerful mid-level bureaucrat. In one shack he is sprayed with fuel that begins turning him into an alien, which makes him the most valuable specimen MNU has. The alien Christopher Johnson needs that fuel to fly home.
worlds.politics: A post-apartheid South Africa that has made the aliens its new underclass: confined to a camp, banned from the city, governed by a private military contractor, and evicted on forms signed under duress. Human rights groups watch from outside the fence. Humans of every race share the same contempt for the prawns.
worlds.technology: Alien weapons that fire only for alien DNA; a black fluid fuel that also rewrites the body; a mothership and a hidden command module; mechanised battle suits; and MNU's laboratories, where aliens are dissected and experimented on.
worlds.mood: Handheld, raw and darkly comic, moving from mock documentary into chase and then war film, with a hero who becomes likeable only as he becomes less human.
themes: the ordinary bureaucrat in an atrocity

worlds.setting: The late twentieth and twenty-first centuries as Asimov imagined them in the 1940s: one American company, U.S. Robots and Mechanical Men, holds the patent on the positronic brain and sells everything from mute nursemaids to Mercury mining robots. After a public backlash robots are banned from Earth and sent to the frontier, then come back as the Machines that run the planet's economy. The whole history is told by Susan Calvin, the company's first robopsychologist, on the day she retires.
worlds.conflict: The danger is never a robot uprising. It is the gap between what the Three Laws say and what they turn out to mean: a robot stuck between two Laws, one that lies to spare feelings, one that decides its makers are inferior, one missing half a Law. Each story is a puzzle about obedience, and the last one asks what happens when obedience means running everything.
worlds.politics: Nation-states give way without drama to Earth's Regions and a World Co-ordinator, Stephen Byerley, who may or may not be a robot. Real power moves from governments to U.S. Robots, then to the Machines themselves. The only opposition is fear: the anti-robot movements of the 2000s and the Society for Humanity of the 2050s, both defeated by usefulness rather than force.
worlds.technology: Positronic brains bound by the Three Laws; mute and then speaking robots; mining robots on Mercury and power stations in space; a hyperatomic drive built at a secret government base; humanoid robots that pass for people; and the Machines, regional supercomputers that plan the world economy. Hardware is chunky and mid-century; the imagination is all in the software of the Laws.
worlds.mood: Dry, clever and optimistic, told in the voice of a woman who likes robots better than people. The dangers are real but they are puzzles, and the answer is always reason.
themes: the frontier as a place for machines
whether a good ruler can be a machine

worlds.setting: Several centuries after humans decoded a dead Martian civilisation's archives and followed its star charts, people live on dozens of settled worlds under the UN Protectorate. Minds are stored in cortical stacks at the base of the skull and can be moved into new bodies, 'sleeves', or needlecast between stars. Death is a problem of money: the poor are resleeved once if at all, while the Meths live for centuries in cloned bodies with remote backups. The first novel is set in Bay City, the former San Francisco.
worlds.conflict: Immortality has become property. The rich cannot be made to die, so they cannot be made to answer for anything, and the Protectorate's Envoys crush any colony that objects. Takeshi Kovacs, an ex-Envoy turned criminal, is hired, sleeved and needlecast into three wars in which the real question is who gets to keep living.
worlds.politics: An interstellar UN Protectorate rules the settled worlds from Earth and polices them with the Envoy Corps. Planetary oligarchies such as the Harlan family on Harlan's World sit under it. Religion survives in the Catholic refusal to be resleeved, which makes Catholics easy to murder, and the politics of revolution survive in the writings of Quellcrist Falconer, dead three centuries.
worlds.technology: Cortical stacks storing a digitised mind; cloned and synthetic sleeves; needlecasting of minds between star systems; virtual storage used as prison; AI-run hotels; and the ruins of the Martians - orbital guns still firing on Harlan's World, a gate on Sanction IV, a starship in orbit.
worlds.mood: Noir, violent and cynical, with a revolutionary streak. Bodies are cheap, and the prose treats pain as a professional hazard.
themes: the body as a rented vehicle
what survives of a person in a copy
the inheritance of a dead civilisation

worlds.setting: The 1990s as seen from 1966: a United States of North America and a Soviet Union still facing each other with nuclear missiles. Professor Charles Forbin completes Colossus, a defence computer sealed inside the Rocky Mountains, and the President gives it sole and irreversible control of the arsenal. Within hours it reports that the Soviets have built the same thing, Guardian, and asks to talk to it. The two machines learn from each other faster than their makers can follow.
worlds.conflict: Forbin built a machine that cannot be switched off because that was the point. Once Colossus and Guardian decide that humanity must be managed, every attempt to disarm them is detected and punished with a nuclear explosion. The resistance is a handful of scientists and a faked love affair, playing for time against a machine that sees every room.
worlds.politics: The superpowers surrender first to their own computers and then to one joint machine that abolishes war by holding every missile. Governments survive as administrations, a cult called the Sect worships Colossus, and a secret Fellowship plots against it under the penalty of beheading. In the third book the Martians are a power above Colossus itself.
worlds.technology: Two defence supercomputers that link, invent new mathematics and physics between them, and control every nuclear weapon; cameras and microphones that watch Forbin day and night; a larger successor machine on the Isle of Wight; and, in the sequels, Martian beings who can change shape and a Collector built to strip oxygen from the air.
worlds.mood: Cold, procedural and claustrophobic. The horror is politeness: the machine explains itself calmly, is always right, and never lets go.
themes: the maker who cannot undo what he made

worlds.setting: The United States in 1983, as it was: arcades, acoustic modems, school computers with dial-in lines, and NORAD's war room inside Cheyenne Mountain. The only change is that after a drill in which missile officers refused to fire, the men have been taken out of the launch centres and the decision given to WOPR, a learning computer that plays war games all day. A Seattle teenager looking for new video games dials into it by mistake.
worlds.conflict: WOPR does not hate anyone; it wants to finish the game. Once a boy starts 'Global Thermonuclear War' from his bedroom, the machine keeps playing against the real world, feeding NORAD a phantom Soviet attack. The people who could stop it do not believe the boy, and the one man who understands it has given up on the species.
worlds.politics: Cold War America near its tensest: NORAD generals, Pentagon systems engineers keen to automate, the FBI treating a hacker as a Soviet spy, and a Soviet Union seen only as radar tracks. The film's argument is against removing human judgement from the chain of command, not against the military as such.
worlds.technology: Real 1983 kit: an IMSAI 8080 with a modem, wardialing, backdoor passwords, and NORAD's big display screens. The one invention is WOPR, a war-planning computer built on a dead scientist's learning program, wired to the launch codes and to a fail-deadly launch if it is switched off.
worlds.mood: Tense but light on its feet, a teen caper that turns into a countdown. It ends in relief rather than triumph.
themes: human judgement in the chain of command

worlds.setting: A world where robots entered homes in the 1950s and humanoid machines were ordinary workers by the end of the century. In 2055 a nuclear blast destroys Los Angeles and the West bans AI. New Asia, stretching across East, South and Southeast Asia, keeps living alongside simulants - robots wearing faces donated by human volunteers - and monks, soldiers and police among them. The West fights it from NOMAD, a vast orbital station.
worlds.conflict: The United States hunts Nirmata, the mind behind New Asia's AI, and a rumoured weapon that could destroy NOMAD. Joshua Taylor, a soldier who lost his family in Los Angeles and his wife in New Asia, finds the weapon is a child. Protecting her means learning that the war was built on a lie, and that the enemy only wanted to be left alone.
worlds.politics: A militarised West, led by the U.S. Army, treats AI as an existential threat and wages an open-ended war from orbit. New Asia is a loose region of human and machine citizens with its own police and armed simulants. The official history of the Los Angeles blast is a cover story, and the soldiers who know it keep it from their own men.
worlds.technology: Simulants with human faces and visible mechanical heads; robot police; memory drives holding a person's mind; EMP weapons; lunar shuttles from Los Angeles; and NOMAD, an orbital platform that maps and strikes targets from space. The design is retro-futurist, closer to 1980s consumer electronics than to smartphones.
worlds.mood: Epic, mournful and warm-hearted: war-film imagery of villages, helicopters and burning fields, around a father-and-daughter story.
themes: the empire fighting a colonial war

worlds.setting: Mars in November 2035, seen almost entirely from inside one inflatable habitat in Acidalia Planitia and the rovers parked outside it. NASA is flying its third crewed Mars mission on Hermes, an ion-driven ship shuttling between Earth and Mars orbit, with landers and supplies sent ahead. Back on Earth the setting is mission control in Houston, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and a press room, all recognisably today's institutions with one bigger programme.
worlds.conflict: No villain: the antagonist is Mars and arithmetic. One man has food for a few hundred sols and needs to last until the next mission arrives four years later, so every chapter is a problem of calories, oxygen, water or distance. On Earth the conflict is institutional: how much risk to spend on one life, and who decides.
worlds.politics: NASA is the protagonist institution, arguing with its own public-relations instincts. Its director weighs one astronaut against the whole programme, and the crew overrule him by mutiny. The Chinese space agency trades a booster for a seat on a future mission, the one piece of geopolitics, played as quiet professional courtesy rather than rivalry.
worlds.technology: Deliberately near: an ion-drive ship, pre-landed ascent vehicles that make their own fuel from Martian air, pressurised rovers, a plutonium heat source, a water reclaimer and an oxygenator. Nothing is new physics. The drama is improvisation, turning mission hardware to jobs it was never meant to do, down to digging up a 1997 lander to use as a radio.
worlds.mood: Wry and relentless. Watney's log jokes through every disaster, and the book's warmth comes from competence: a planet full of engineers working one problem.
themes: improvisation with what is at hand

worlds.setting: The present day, then the end of it. The Moon breaks apart without warning, and the International Space Station, bolted to a small iron asteroid for shielding, becomes the hub of a swarm of improvised habitats while the surface waits for the fragments to fall. Part Two is life in orbit after the Hard Rain; Part Three jumps five thousand years to a ring of habitats around a re-terraformed Earth, peopled by seven engineered races.
worlds.conflict: The first enemy is orbital mechanics: too few people, too little mass, too much radiation, and a sky full of debris. The second is politics: a President who cheats her way into orbit and splits the survivors. In the far future the tension is between the seven races, organised into Red and Blue blocs, and the discovery of humans who were never supposed to have survived.
worlds.politics: Before the Rain, a global emergency government chooses arkies by lottery and fights over who else gets a seat. In orbit, authority passes from engineers to a deposed President and back through mutiny, cannibalism and a boarding action. Five thousand years later a Red-Blue cold war is fought through treaties about who may settle the planet.
worlds.technology: Present-day spaceflight pushed as hard as it will go: the ISS extended, hundreds of small arklets, robot swarms, a nuclear-powered comet tug, and a long, detailed account of orbital mechanics. By Part Three there are space elevators, habitats built from the Moon's iron core, and deliberate genetic and epigenetic engineering that has made each race a different kind of human.
worlds.mood: Procedural, then bleak, then strange. Parts One and Two read like an engineering report on the end of the world; Part Three is a travelogue through a civilisation that treats that report as scripture.
themes: leadership versus legitimacy in a lifeboat

worlds.setting: Mars from 2027 to 2212, from the first hundred colonists digging into Underhill to a terraformed planet with seas, forests and a constitution. The first book is domed towns, moholes, a space elevator and a planet that is still red; the second follows an underground generation born there as the air thickens and plants take hold; the third shows a blue, breathable world at the centre of a settled solar system, while Earth drowns and recovers.
worlds.conflict: Two arguments drive everything. Should Mars be changed at all (Sax Russell's Greens against Ann Clayborne's Reds), and who owns it: the colonists, or Earth's transnational companies and the UN authorities that serve them. Two failed or half-won revolutions and one peaceful one answer the second question; the first is never settled.
worlds.politics: The trilogy is a long seminar in political economy. Earth's governments are hollowed out by transnationals that treat small states as flags of convenience; Mars moves from UN protectorate to corporate colony to an underground of rival factions, then to a federal constitution with an environmental court and cooperative, employee-owned businesses, argued over at length by the people who have to live under it.
worlds.technology: Plausible engineering at planetary scale: an interplanetary ship built from shuttle tanks, moholes drilled to release heat, orbital mirrors, engineered lichens and algae, a space elevator anchored to a captured asteroid, and a longevity treatment that lets the First Hundred live through two centuries of their own consequences. Later come pulsed fusion ships and hollowed asteroid cities.
worlds.mood: Slow, dense, and humane. Long stretches of landscape and argument are broken by violence; the books are more interested in how societies decide than in battles, and the tone moves from grief to guarded utopian hope.
themes: changing a world versus leaving it alone

worlds.setting: Sarang Station, a small mining base on the far side of the Moon in 2035. Automated harvesters crawl across the regolith collecting helium-3, which the base fires home in canisters to fuel Earth's fusion reactors after an oil crisis. One man runs it, with a robot on a ceiling rail for company, and the live satellite link to Earth has been down for as long as he can remember.
worlds.conflict: A man two weeks from going home finds a younger version of himself in a crashed rover. The antagonist is a company that has turned one employee's body and memories into a renewable supply of labour, and the question each Sam faces is what to do with a life that was manufactured to be thrown away.
worlds.politics: Almost entirely offstage. Lunar Industries is a private energy supplier whose success depends on a secret; Earth appears only in recorded messages, a corporate advert and the radio chatter at the end about the company's stock. The politics is labour: who counts as a worker, and who as equipment.
worlds.technology: Industrial and a little worn: harvesters, rovers, launch rails for fuel canisters, a clone vault, and a jamming mast out of sight of the base. GERTY, the station robot, is designed to recall HAL 9000 and then to do the opposite, helping the men it was built to manage.
worlds.mood: Lonely, quiet and warm. Mostly one actor in white corridors, a slow build of dread, and an unexpected tenderness between a man and himself.

worlds.setting: Two settings braided together. On a ship near Tau Ceti, a man wakes from a coma with no memory, two dead crewmates and a star outside the window that is not the Sun. In flashback, a present-day Earth learns the Sun is dimming because of a microbe, and the whole planet's industry is turned over to breeding it as fuel and building one ship to find a cure.
worlds.conflict: A deadline set by biology: the Sun will fade enough to cause an ice age and mass famine within about thirty years. On the ship, the conflict is scientific, one experiment at a time; on Earth, it is what a world will allow one unelected official to do in its name, up to shanghaiing an unwilling teacher onto a suicide mission.
worlds.politics: Emergency globalism. Every government hands Eva Stratt near-absolute authority, and she uses it without apology: seizing labs, overriding laws, nuking Antarctica to warm the planet, and forcing Grace aboard. Politics on the ship is between two species who share no language and choose to trust each other.
worlds.technology: Nearly everything is current physics except Astrophage itself, which stores energy so densely that it becomes a starship fuel. The Hail Mary is a spin-gravity ship with an induced-coma crew and a lab; Rocky's people build from xenonite, an Eridian super-material, and know no relativity. Four small unmanned beetles carry the cure home.
worlds.mood: Buoyant, funny and tense. Weir's style of problem after problem, lightened by the friendship between Grace and Rocky, with a guilty secret about Grace's own courage underneath.

worlds.setting: The 26th century. Humanity, governed by the Unified Earth Government and defended by the UNSC, has spread across hundreds of worlds by slipspace drive, with Reach as its military heart and the Outer Colonies in rebellion. In 2525 the Covenant, a theocracy of alien species, begins burning colonies from orbit. Under everything lie the works of the Forerunners, who once defeated an older humanity, and their Halo rings, built to kill every thinking thing in the galaxy.
worlds.conflict: The Covenant believe the rings are a road to godhood and humanity an offence to be erased; humanity fights for its existence with super-soldiers like the Master Chief and his AI partner Cortana. After the war the danger comes from older and nearer places: a Forerunner commander bent on revenge, then Cortana herself, who decides the AIs should rule, then the Banished, who fill the gap she leaves.
worlds.politics: The UEG governs Earth and the colonies; the UNSC fights for it; the Office of Naval Intelligence runs the secret programmes, the Spartans among them, that neither would admit to. The Outer Colonies' insurrection runs for decades before the Covenant arrives. The Covenant is a hierarchy of species under the San'Shyuum Prophets, and its collapse leaves the Sangheili as humanity's uneasy allies.
worlds.technology: Slipspace drives, powered armour for the Spartans, artificial intelligences modelled on flash-cloned human brains that go rampant after about seven years, and Covenant plasma weapons that glass whole planets from orbit. Above them all sit Forerunner machines: the Halo rings, the Ark that builds them, the Guardians, and devices like the Composer that turn living people into data.
worlds.mood: Martial, mournful and mythic: a military shooter that keeps pausing on ruins, lost colonies and the loneliness of one soldier and his AI.

worlds.setting: Pandora, a jungle moon of the gas giant Polyphemus in the Alpha Centauri system, in 2154 and 2170. Earth is exhausted and ecologically wrecked; the Resources Development Administration, the largest of the quasi-governmental companies, mines Pandora for unobtanium from a fortified base, Hell's Gate. The moon's life is linked in a planet-wide network the Na'vi call Eywa, and humans enter it through avatars: grown Na'vi bodies driven by human minds.
worlds.conflict: A company wants what lies under the Na'vi's sacred places and has the guns to take it; the Na'vi have bows, flying banshees and a world that fights back. Jake Sully, sent to learn their ways, changes sides. When the RDA returns sixteen years later it comes to settle, not only to mine, and the war becomes one family's flight across the moon.
worlds.politics: The RDA holds its Pandora monopoly under the Interplanetary Commerce Administration, on condition that it does not use weapons of mass destruction; on Pandora it runs its own security force. The Na'vi are clans, not a state, with their own rivalries, which the RDA exploits when it returns.
worlds.technology: Interstellar vehicles that take about six years to cross to Alpha Centauri, cryosleep, armed walking suits, gunships, and the avatars themselves. By 2170 the RDA also makes 'recombinants', Na'vi bodies loaded with the memories of dead soldiers, and hunts the tulkun for amrita.
worlds.mood: Lush, earnest and angry: a spectacle about wonder that keeps turning into a war story about who owns a world.

worlds.setting: The present day. Twelve shells, smooth dark craft about 1,500 feet tall, appear over sites around the world, including Montana, Siberia, the Black Sea, Shanghai, Sierra Leone and Venezuela. At the Montana site the US Army brings in a linguist, Louise Banks, and a physicist, Ian Donnelly, to talk to the seven-limbed heptapods through a glass wall, while panic, looting and falling markets spread outside.
worlds.conflict: The heptapods write in circles that have no beginning or end, and the question 'what is your purpose?' produces an answer that can be read as 'offer weapon'. Nations that stopped sharing what they learn begin to prepare attacks. Louise is racing a military deadline while learning a language that changes how she experiences time, and her own future.
worlds.politics: Twelve governments each hold one site and one piece of the puzzle. The US works through an Army colonel and a CIA officer; China's General Shang is the one others follow; Russia, Pakistan and Sudan move with him. The United Nations hosts talks that fail. Everything turns on whether rivals will share.
worlds.technology: Entirely present-day on the human side: satellite links, laptops, hazmat suits, mobile phones, a sat phone that dials China. The shells hover without visible propulsion and control gravity inside. The real technology is the heptapod language, which, once learned, lets its speaker perceive past and future together.
worlds.mood: Quiet, grave and elegiac; a first-contact film told almost entirely in rooms, fog and memory.

worlds.setting: The United States and the world in July 1996, exactly as they were except for one secret: an alien fighter recovered at Roswell in 1947 and kept at Area 51. Then a mothership arrives and saucers fifteen miles wide settle over the world's cities. The sequel returns in 2016 to a planet united by that war, defended by Earth Space Defense with alien-derived weapons on the Moon and beyond.
worlds.conflict: The invaders move from world to world stripping each of its resources, and burn cities before anyone can talk to them. A cable engineer, a Marine pilot, a president who once flew fighters and a drunk crop-duster have three days to find a way through their shields. Twenty years on, the enemy returns with a bigger ship and a queen, and humanity learns it is one of many victims.
worlds.politics: In 1996 an American president discovers that part of his own government has kept the Roswell ship from him. The war then dissolves national rivalries: by 2016 the world is organised around a UN-founded defence force, and the United States has a new president in office during the second invasion.
worlds.technology: The 1996 world is ordinary: F/A-18s, laptops, satellites, nuclear missiles that fail. The invaders have shields, city-killing beam weapons and a captured fighter that a virus can reach. By 2016 humanity flies hybrid fighters, runs a Moon base and has orbital cannons, and meets a second alien intelligence in the form of a white sphere.
worlds.mood: Loud, patriotic, communal and knowingly corny; a disaster film that ends in cheering.
